description.en: Ysgithyrwyn Chief Boar (Gwen Jones tr.), Yskithyrwyn Benbaedd (Lady Guest tr.) (Welsh: Ysgithrwyn Pen Beidd, Yskithyrwynn Pennbeidd; Middle Welsh: yskithyrwyn penn beird, RBH; ẏskithẏr6ẏn WBR) or "White-tusk chief of Boars" is another boar being hunted, secondary to the great boar Twrch Trwyth by the Arthur's wild chase party in the Welsh Arthurian romance Culhwch ac Olwen. Its tusk (Welsh: ysgithyr) was the necessary implement for shaving the giant Ysbaddaden Chief-Giant. Ysbaddaden proclaimed this tusk was no use to him unless extracted from the boar while still alive, and only Odgar the son of Aedd the king of Ireland was capable of accomplishing this. This boar was slain (or at least chased down and cornered into inevitable death) not "by the dogs that Yspaddaden had mentioned, but by Cavall, Arthur's own dog.". In fact it was Kaw of North Britain (Cadw of Pydein, or Pictland), who, mounted on Arthur's mare Llamrei swung a battle-axe or hatchet (Welsh: bwyellic, bwyellig) at the boar and spliced its head. Thus it remains dubious whether the extraction of the tusk took place as the giant prescribed (i.e., while the boar was alive, or undertaken by Odgar). But Cadw/Kaw took charge of the tusk, in keeping with Arthur' earlier vow that no other would be entrusted with its care.

description.en: Zână (plural zâne; zînă and zîne, d̦ână and d̦âne in old spellings) is the Romanian equivalent of the Greek Charites or the fairy godmother. They are the opposite of monsters such as Muma Pădurii. These characters make positive appearances in fairy tales and mostly reside in the woods. They can also be considered the Romanian equivalent of fairies and the Germanic elf. They vary in size and appearance and can transform to blend into their surroundings for protection and cover. They can appear openly in the woods and coax travelers to follow them in order to help them find their way. They can also hide in the woods and quietly guide those who need help through signs and "breadcrumbs" through the forest.

description.en: Zburător or sburător (Romanian word meaning 'flyer') is a supernatural being in Romanian folklore, described as a "roving spirit who makes love to maidens by night".

claims.statement: Zburător or sburător (Romanian for "flyer") is a supernatural being of Romanian folklore, a "roving spirit who makes love to maidens by night".
claims.statement_id: Zburător atau sburător (kata Rumania yang berarti "yang terbang") adalah makhluk gaib dalam cerita rakyat Rumania, "roh pengembara yang bercinta dengan gadis-gadis pada malam hari".
claims.quote: or sburător (Romanian word meaning 'flyer') is a supernatural being in Romanian folklore, described as a "roving spirit who makes love to maidens by night".

claims.statement: The zburător is likened to an incubus, a malevolent demon visiting women in dreams in the guise of a handsome young man.
claims.statement_id: Zburător disamakan dengan inkubus, iblis jahat yang mendatangi perempuan dalam mimpi dengan menyamar sebagai pemuda tampan.
claims.quote: The zburător is also likened to an incubus, and described as a malevolent demon active in a "oniric-erotic" manner, i.e., visiting women in their dreams in the guise of a handsome young man.

claims.statement: A zburător may also be a specific form a zmeu takes; in some regions it is called a zmeu.
claims.statement_id: Zburător bisa juga merupakan wujud tertentu dari zmeu; di beberapa daerah ia disebut zmeu.
claims.quote: A zburător may also be a specific form that a zmeu can take.

claims.statement: Dimitrie Cantemir in Descriptio Moldaviae (1714–1716) recorded the Moldavian belief that he was a ghost, a handsome youth coming at midnight to women, especially newlyweds, unseen by others.
claims.statement_id: Dimitrie Cantemir dalam Descriptio Moldaviae (1714–1716) mencatat kepercayaan orang Moldavia bahwa ia hantu berupa pemuda tampan yang datang tengah malam kepada perempuan, terutama pengantin baru, dan tidak dapat dilihat orang lain.
claims.quote: "a ghost, a young, handsome man who comes in the middle of the night at women, especially recently married ones and does indecent things with them, although he cannot be seen by other people, not even by the ones who waylay him".

claims.statement: A literary reworking appeared in Ion Heliade Rădulescu's romantic poem Zburătorul (1843).
claims.statement_id: Pengolahan sastra mitos ini muncul dalam puisi romantis Ion Heliade Rădulescu, Zburătorul (1843).
claims.quote: A literary reworking of the myth later appeared in the romantic poem by Ion Heliade Rădulescu Zburătorul ('The Flyer/Flying Incubus', 1843)

claims.statement: According to George Călinescu's classification, the zburător, with the Miorița epic and the legends of Master Manole and Baba Dochia, is one of the four fundamental Romanian myths.
claims.statement_id: Menurut klasifikasi George Călinescu, zburător, bersama epos Miorița dan legenda Meșterul Manole serta Baba Dochia, adalah salah satu dari empat mitos dasar Rumania.
claims.quote: Според класификацията на Джордже Кълинеску е, заедно с епоса Миорица и легендите за майстор Манол и Баба Докия – един от четирите основни румънски мита.

description.en: Zhytsen or Žycień (Belarusian: Жыцень) is a positive creature from Belarusian mythology said to live in fields. The name literally means "rye creature", from Belarusian жыта, "rye".

claims.statement: Zhytsen or Žycień is a benevolent creature of Belarusian mythology said to live in fields; the name literally means "rye creature", from Belarusian zhyta, "rye".
claims.statement_id: Zhytsen atau Žycień adalah makhluk baik dalam mitologi Belarus yang konon tinggal di ladang; namanya secara harfiah berarti "makhluk gandum hitam", dari kata Belarus zhyta, "gandum hitam".
claims.quote: is a positive creature from Belarusian mythology said to live in fields. The name literally means "rye creature", from Belarusian жыта, "rye".

claims.statement: Zhytsen is often called a spirit of wealth and wellbeing; it is believed to help crops and vegetables ripen well and so is considered the caretaker of good harvests.
claims.statement_id: Zhytsen sering disebut roh kekayaan dan kesejahteraan; ia dipercaya membantu tanaman dan sayuran matang dengan baik, sehingga dianggap pengurus panen yang baik.
claims.quote: Zhyten is often called a spirit of wealth and wellbeing. It is believed that Zhytsen contributes to good ripening of crops and vegetables, and accordingly, Zhyten is considered the caretaker of good harvests.

claims.statement: Zhytsen walks the fields making sure the crops are well reaped; Belarusian folklore holds that if it finds ears of grain left behind, it binds them into sheaves and carries them to the fields of more diligent farmers.
claims.statement_id: Zhytsen berjalan melintasi ladang memastikan panen dituai dengan baik; dalam folklor Belarus dipercaya bila ia menemukan bulir yang tertinggal, ia mengikatnya menjadi berkas dan membawanya ke ladang petani yang lebih rajin.
claims.quote: Zhytsen walks through the fields and ensures that crops there are well reaped. It is believed in Belarusian folklore that if Zhytsen finds some left ears of grain, it binds them in sheaves and brings to the fields of more diligent farmers.

claims.statement: As an ancient Belarusian god of fertility and autumn, Zhytsen was described, and probably invented, by the folklorist Pavel Shpilevsky (Drevlyansky).
claims.statement_id: Sebagai dewa kesuburan dan musim gugur Belarus kuno, Zhytsen digambarkan, dan kemungkinan dikarang, oleh folkloris Pavel Shpilevsky (Drevlyansky).
claims.quote: Как древнебелорусский бог плодородия и осени описан (и, вероятно, придуман) фольклористом Павлом Шпилевским (Древлянским).

claims.statement: A peculiarity of Zhytsen is a third eye on the back of the head, which helps it do its work better.
claims.statement_id: Ciri khas Zhytsen adalah mata ketiga di tengkuk, yang membantunya menjalankan tugasnya dengan lebih baik.
claims.quote: Особенностью Житеня является третий глаз на затылке, который нужен для лучшего выполнения задач этого мифологического персонажа.

claims.statement: In Belarus Zhytsen was imagined as a little old man ("Rye Grandfather") with a long beard.
claims.statement_id: Di Belarus, Zhytsen dibayangkan sebagai kakek kecil ("Kakek Gandum Hitam") berjanggut panjang.
claims.quote: На Беларусі Жыценя уяўлялі маленькім дзедам («Жытні дзед») з доўгай барадой.

claims.statement: The figure of Zhytsen still appears in Belarusian folklore, for example in the saying "Zhytsen gave bread".
claims.statement_id: Sosok Zhytsen masih tampak dalam folklor Belarus, antara lain dalam ungkapan "Zhytsen memberi roti".
claims.quote: Образ Жиценя й досі спостерігається в білоруському фольклорі, зокрема в примовці «Жыцень хлеба дав».

description.en: The zmeu (plural: zmei, feminine: zmeoaică / zmeoaice) is a fantastic creature of Romanian folklore and Romanian mythology. Though referred by some sources as a dragon, the zmeu is nevertheless distinct, because it usually has clear anthropomorphic traits: it is humanoid and has legs, arms, the ability to create and use artifacts such as weapons, and to ride a horse, and has the desire to marry young girls. There are commentators that class it as a giant (equivalent of an ogre), or a devil, or even a vampire. In some stories, Zmeu appears in the sky and spits fire, or has the ability to change form. In other stories, it has a magical precious stone on its head that shines like the sun. It likes beautiful young girls, whom it kidnaps, usually for the purpose of marrying them. It is almost always defeated by a daring prince or knight-errant. The zmeu has also been conflated with or confused with the dracu or with the balaur type dragon. Various stories say that he is slain by a young prince, like Prâslea cel voinic(the mighty Prâslea)

claims.statement: The zmeu (plural zmei, feminine zmeoaică) is a fantastic creature of Romanian folklore and mythology.
claims.statement_id: Zmeu (jamak zmei, perempuan zmeoaică) adalah makhluk fantastis dalam cerita rakyat dan mitologi Rumania.
claims.quote: is a fantastic creature of Romanian folklore and Romanian mythology.

claims.statement: Though some sources call it a dragon, the zmeu is distinct for its human-like traits: legs, arms, making and using weapons, riding a horse and wishing to marry young girls; some commentators class it as a giant (ogre), a devil or a vampire.
claims.statement_id: Walau sebagian sumber menyebutnya naga, zmeu berbeda karena bersifat manusia: berkaki, berlengan, membuat dan memakai senjata, menunggang kuda, dan ingin menikahi gadis muda; ada pengulas yang menggolongkannya sebagai raksasa (ogre), iblis, atau vampir.
claims.quote: Though referred by some sources as a dragon, the zmeu is nevertheless distinct, because it usually has clear anthropomorphic traits: it is humanoid and has legs, arms, the ability to create and use artifacts such as weapons, and to ride a horse, and has the desire to marry young girls. There are commentators that class it as a giant (equivalent of an ogre), or a devil, or even a vampire.

claims.statement: In some stories the zmeu appears in the sky and spits fire or can change form; in others it has a magic gem on its head shining like the sun.
claims.statement_id: Dalam beberapa cerita zmeu muncul di langit dan menyemburkan api, atau dapat berubah wujud; dalam cerita lain ia punya batu permata ajaib di kepala yang bersinar seperti matahari.
claims.quote: In some stories, Zmeu appears in the sky and spits fire, or has the ability to change form. In other stories, it has a magical precious stone on its head that shines like the sun.

claims.statement: It likes beautiful young girls and kidnaps them, usually to marry them, and is almost always defeated by a daring prince or knight-errant.
claims.statement_id: Ia menyukai gadis muda yang cantik dan menculiknya, biasanya untuk dinikahi, dan hampir selalu dikalahkan pangeran atau kesatria pemberani.
claims.quote: It likes beautiful young girls, whom it kidnaps, usually for the purpose of marrying them. It is almost always defeated by a daring prince or knight-errant.

claims.statement: Most scholars agree the Romanian term zmeu derives from Slavic zmey.
claims.statement_id: Kebanyakan sarjana sepakat istilah Rumania zmeu berasal dari kata Slavia zmey.
claims.quote: Most scholars agree that the Romanian term zmeu derives from Slavic zmey.

claims.statement: In Romanian mythology the zmeu is a giant being with supernatural powers, the embodiment of evil, always defeated by the forces of good.
claims.statement_id: Dalam mitologi Rumania, zmeu adalah makhluk raksasa berkekuatan gaib, perwujudan kejahatan, yang selalu dikalahkan oleh kekuatan baik.
claims.quote: En la mitología rumana, un esmeuro o dracosmeu (en rumano zmeu) es un ser gigante con poderes sobrenaturales, encarnación del mal, pero que siempre es derrotado por las fuerzas del bien

claims.statement: In Romanian the word zmeu also means the kites children fly.
claims.statement_id: Kata zmeu dalam bahasa Rumania juga berarti layang-layang yang diterbangkan anak-anak.
claims.quote: La palabra también se refiere a las cometas que vuelan los niños dado que la palabra zmeu también significa cometa en rumano.

claims.statement: The zmeu has also been conflated with the dracu or the balaur dragon; various stories have it slain by a young prince like Prâslea cel voinic.
claims.statement_id: Zmeu juga dikacaukan dengan dracu atau naga jenis balaur; dalam berbagai cerita ia dibunuh pangeran muda seperti Prâslea cel voinic.
claims.quote: The zmeu has also been conflated with or confused with the dracu or with the balaur type dragon. ... like Prâslea cel voinic
